key_insight: Multi-agent collaboration is not always better: for capable language models, adding more agents or coordination can sometimes reduce performance instead of improving it. The paper shows these tradeoffs can be predicted well enough to choose the best setup in most within-domain cases.
problem_solved: It addresses the practical question of when multi-agent language model systems actually help, and when they introduce overhead, redundancy, or conflict that harms results.
method: Ran a controlled study over 260 multi-agent configuration settings.
Compared performance across different collaboration architectures to identify conditions where collaboration helps or hurts.
Trained a predictive model to recommend the best architecture for a given setting, achieving 87% accuracy on held-out within-domain configurations.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this helps avoid assuming that more agents automatically means better performance. It provides a data-driven way to design multi-agent systems more efficiently and select the right architecture for a task.
visual_elements: Split-path diagram showing 'single agent' vs 'multi-agent collaboration' outcomes
Heatmap of 260 configurations highlighting where collaboration helps or hurts
Flowchart of the predictive architecture-selection model

paper_title: Capable language models can outgrow the benefits of collaboration
paper_authors: Yubin Kim, Ken Gu, Chanwoo Park, Chunjong Park, Samuel Schmidgall
